content: Functional training has been shown to significantly reduce the rate of falls and the risk of injuries resulting from falls in older adults aged 65 years and above. This is particularly evident when comparing individuals who engage in multicomponent physical activity programs to those who do not. Such programs are associated with improved balance, strength, and overall physical function, which are critical for fall prevention. Sedentary behavior, defined as time spent sitting or lying down with minimal energy expenditure while awake, is associated with poor health outcomes in older adults. These outcomes include increased all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type-2 diabetes. It is strongly recommended that older adults limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activities, to gain health benefits. Engaging in more than the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity can further mitigate the negative effects of prolonged sedentary behavior. For pregnant and postpartum women, physical activity is highly beneficial for both maternal and fetal health. Regular physical activity during pregnancy reduces the risk of complications such as pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive gestational weight gain, delivery complications, and postpartum depression. It also leads to fewer complications for newborns without adversely affecting birth weight or increasing the risk of stillbirth. Pregnant women are encouraged to engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, incorporating a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening exercises. Gentle stretching may also be beneficial. Women who were habitually active before pregnancy can continue their vigorous-intensity activities during pregnancy and postpartum, provided there are no contraindications. Concerns about potential adverse effects of maternal physical activity on the developing fetus or delivery outcomes have been largely dispelled by recent evidence. Physical activity does not increase the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, or delivery complications. It is also not associated with an increased incidence of cesarean delivery, even in women with overweight or obesity. Furthermore, physical activity during pregnancy is inversely associated with postpartum depression and may reduce the risk of preterm birth for mothers engaging in vigorous-intensity activities. For adults and older adults living with chronic conditions such as cancer, hypertension, type-2 diabetes, and HIV, physical activity offers substantial health benefits. In cancer survivors, it improves all-cause mortality, cancer-specific mortality, and reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or secondary cancers. For individuals with hypertension, physical activity improves cardiovascular disease mortality, disease progression, physical function, and health-related quality of life. In those with type-2 diabetes, it reduces cardiovascular disease mortality and slows disease progression. For people living with HIV, physical activity enhances physical fitness and mental health, reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression, without adversely affecting disease progression (e.g., CD4 count or viral load) or body composition. The WHO guidelines emphasize that all adults, including those with chronic conditions, should aim to meet the recommended 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. Physical activity can be undertaken in various forms, including recreational activities, transportation (e.g., walking or cycling), occupational tasks, or household chores. Even small amounts of physical activity are better than none, and individuals are encouraged to start with manageable levels and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. The benefits of physical activity far outweigh the risks, even for those with chronic conditions, provided there are no contraindications.
